title: Directive Principles of State Policy
desc: Non-justiciable state goals guiding governance and justice

basic.q: Which Part of the Constitution contains the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)?
basic.e: The Directive Principles of State Policy are contained in Part IV of the Constitution, from Articles 36 to 51.

basic.q: The Directive Principles of State Policy were borrowed from the Constitution of which country?
basic.e: The concept of DPSP was borrowed from the Irish Constitution, which had in turn borrowed it from the Spanish Constitution.

basic.q: Which Article of the Constitution declares that the Directive Principles shall not be enforceable by any court?
basic.e: Article 37 states that the DPSPs are not enforceable by any court but are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country.

basic.q: Article 36 of the Constitution deals with which of the following?
basic.e: Article 36 defines the term 'State' for the purposes of Part IV in the same sense as it is defined in Article 12 for Fundamental Rights.

basic.q: Which Article directs the State to secure equal pay for equal work for both men and women?
basic.e: Article 39(d) directs the State to ensure equal pay for equal work for both men and women.

basic.q: Which Article of the Constitution deals with the organization of village panchayats?
basic.e: Article 40 directs the State to take steps to organize village panchayats and endow them with such powers as may be necessary for self-government, forming the basis of the 73rd Amendment.

basic.q: Which Article provides for a living wage for workers?
basic.e: Article 43 directs the State to secure a living wage, decent standard of life, and social and cultural opportunities for workers.

basic.q: Which Article directs the State to endeavour to secure a Uniform Civil Code for citizens?
basic.e: Article 44 directs the State to endeavour to secure a Uniform Civil Code throughout the territory of India.

basic.q: Article 45 of the Constitution, as amended by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002, deals with?
o: Provision for early childhood care and education for children below six years
Free and compulsory education for children of 6-14 years
basic.e: After the 86th Amendment Act, 2002, Article 45 was changed to provide for early childhood care and education for children below the age of six, since free and compulsory education for 6-14 years became a Fundamental Right under Article 21A.

basic.q: Which Article directs the State to promote the educational and economic interests of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other weaker sections?
basic.e: Article 46 directs the State to promote with special care the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections, particularly SCs and STs, and to protect them from social injustice and exploitation.

basic.q: Which Article casts a duty on the State to organize agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines and prohibits slaughter of cows, calves and other milch and draught cattle?
basic.e: Article 48 directs the State to organize agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines and, in particular, to prohibit the slaughter of cows, calves and other milch and draught cattle.

basic.q: Article 48A of the Constitution deals with?
o: Protection of monuments of national importance
Protection and improvement of environment, forests and wildlife
basic.e: Article 48A directs the State to endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wildlife of the country; it was inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.

basic.q: Which Article of the DPSP relates to the protection of monuments and places of national importance?
basic.e: Article 49 directs the State to protect monuments, places and objects of artistic or historic interest declared to be of national importance.

basic.q: Which Article directs the State to take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State?
basic.e: Article 50 directs the State to take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.

basic.q: Which Article of the DPSP relates to the promotion of international peace and security?
basic.e: Article 51 directs the State to endeavour to promote international peace and security, maintain just and honourable relations between nations, and encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration.

intermediate.q: Which of the following DPSPs is classified as a 'Gandhian principle'?
o: Article 50 - Separation of judiciary from executive
intermediate.e: Article 40 (village panchayats) reflects Gandhian philosophy of decentralization and village self-governance, along with Articles 43, 43B, 46, 47 and 48; Articles 44, 50 and 51 fall under the liberal-intellectual category.

intermediate.q: Consider the following DPSPs: 1. Article 39 - distribution of material resources 2. Article 41 - right to work 3. Article 43A - workers' participation in management. Which of these are classified as 'socialist principles'?
intermediate.e: Articles 38, 39, 39A, 41, 42, 43 and 43A reflect the ideology of socialism, aiming to secure social and economic democracy, and are all classified as socialist principles of DPSP.

intermediate.q: Which of the following is correctly classified under the 'liberal-intellectual' category of DPSPs?
o: Article 50 - separation of judiciary from executive
intermediate.e: Article 50 (separation of judiciary from executive), along with Articles 44, 45, 48, 48A, 49 and 51, is classified as a liberal-intellectual principle since it reflects the ideology of liberalism.

intermediate.q: Which of the following statements about the enforceability of Directive Principles is correct?
o: DPSPs are directly enforceable in courts like Fundamental Rights
DPSPs are non-justiciable but fundamental in the governance of the country as per Article 37
DPSPs can only be enforced through Presidential Ordinances
DPSPs override Fundamental Rights in all circumstances
intermediate.e: As per Article 37, the DPSPs are not enforceable by any court, yet the principles laid down are declared to be fundamental in the governance of the country and it is the duty of the State to apply them in making laws.

intermediate.q: The Directive Principles relating to equal justice and free legal aid (Article 39A) and workers' participation in management (Article 43A) were inserted into the Constitution by which amendment?
intermediate.e: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 inserted Articles 39A, 43A and 48A into Part IV, along with Fundamental Duties in a new Part IVA.

intermediate.q: Article 43B, relating to the promotion of cooperative societies, was inserted into the DPSP by which Constitutional Amendment?
intermediate.e: The 97th Amendment Act, 2011 inserted Article 43B, directing the State to promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning and democratic control of cooperative societies.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements: 1. Article 31C was originally inserted by the 25th Amendment Act, 1971. 2. It originally protected only laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and (c) from being challenged as violative of Articles 14 and 19. Which of the statements is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The 25th Amendment Act, 1971 inserted Article 31C, which shielded laws implementing Article 39(b) and (c) from being declared void for violating Articles 14 or 19.

intermediate.q: Which amendment removed the Right to Property from the list of Fundamental Rights and made it a legal right under Article 300A, thereby easing tension with DPSPs relating to distribution of resources?
intermediate.e: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 repealed Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31, converting the right to property into a mere legal right under Article 300A.

intermediate.q: Which of the following best distinguishes Fundamental Rights from Directive Principles of State Policy?
o: Fundamental Rights are found in Part IV while DPSPs are in Part III
Fundamental Rights are justiciable while DPSPs are non-justiciable
DPSPs promote individual liberty while Fundamental Rights promote social welfare
DPSPs can be suspended during a financial emergency while Fundamental Rights cannot
intermediate.e: Fundamental Rights (Part III) are legally enforceable by courts, whereas DPSPs (Part IV) are non-justiciable, being merely directives for governance under Article 37.

intermediate.q: Article 40, which directs organization of village panchayats, became the constitutional basis for which subsequent amendment?
intermediate.e: Article 40's directive to organize village panchayats provided the philosophical basis for the 73rd Amendment Act, 1992, which gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj institutions.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about Article 38: 1. It directs the State to secure a social order for the promotion of welfare of the people. 2. Clause (2) was added by the 44th Amendment to minimize inequalities in income, status and opportunities. Which of the statements is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Article 38(1) directs the State to secure a social order for promoting welfare, while Article 38(2), added by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978, specifically directs minimizing inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities.

intermediate.q: Which of the following DPSP articles was NOT part of the original Constitution of 1950 and was added later by amendment?
o: Article 50 - separation of judiciary from executive
intermediate.e: Article 48A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, along with Fundamental Duties; Articles 39, 44 and 50 were part of the original 1950 Constitution.

intermediate.q: Consider the following pairs of DPSP Article and its subject: 1. Article 41 - Right to work, education and public assistance 2. Article 42 - Provision for just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief 3. Article 47 - Duty of the State to raise the level of nutrition and standard of living. Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
intermediate.e: All three pairs are correctly matched: Article 41 deals with right to work, education and public assistance; Article 42 with humane conditions of work and maternity relief; and Article 47 with nutrition, standard of living and public health.

intermediate.q: The classification of DPSPs into 'socialist', 'Gandhian' and 'liberal-intellectual' categories is a classification made by?
o: The Constitution itself in Part IV
Political scientists/scholars for analytical convenience, not the constitutional text
The Supreme Court in the Kesavananda Bharati case
intermediate.e: The Constitution does not itself classify the DPSPs; the division into socialist, Gandhian and liberal-intellectual principles is a classification adopted by scholars of political science for ease of study and analysis.

intermediate.q: Which of the following is a key difference between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy?
o: Fundamental Rights impose negative obligations restraining the State, while DPSPs impose positive obligations directing the State to act
Fundamental Rights apply only to citizens, while DPSPs apply only to foreigners
DPSPs are found in Part III, while Fundamental Rights are found in Part IV
DPSPs can be enforced through writ petitions under Article 32
intermediate.e: Fundamental Rights are largely negative in character, restraining the State from certain actions, whereas DPSPs are positive instructions directing the State to work towards specific socio-economic goals.

advanced.q: The Supreme Court's decision in State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) primarily held that?
o: DPSPs must always prevail over Fundamental Rights
In case of conflict, Fundamental Rights would prevail over Directive Principles, since DPSPs are non-justiciable
Reservations in education can never be provided by the State
The judiciary has no power of judicial review over any law
advanced.e: In Champakam Dorairajan (1951), the Supreme Court held that in case of a conflict between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs, the former would prevail, since DPSPs are non-justiciable under Article 37 while FRs are enforceable; this led to the First Amendment Act, 1951 inserting Article 15(4).

advanced.q: In I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967), the Supreme Court held that?
o: Parliament has unlimited power to amend any part of the Constitution
Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights, as Article 368 does not give power to abridge Part III
DPSPs are superior to Fundamental Rights
The basic structure doctrine applies retrospectively to all amendments
advanced.e: In Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967), an 11-judge bench held, by a narrow majority, that Parliament could not amend the Fundamental Rights in Part III, applying the doctrine of prospective overruling.

advanced.q: Which Constitutional Amendment was enacted specifically to overcome the effect of the Golaknath judgment by explicitly empowering Parliament to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights?
advanced.e: The 24th Amendment Act, 1971 was passed to nullify the effect of the Golaknath judgment; it amended Article 368 to explicitly empower Parliament to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights.

advanced.q: The 'basic structure doctrine' was propounded by the Supreme Court in which landmark case?
o: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)
Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)
advanced.e: In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), a 13-judge bench of the Supreme Court propounded the basic structure doctrine, holding that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, but cannot alter its basic structure.

advanced.q: The original Article 31C, inserted by the 25th Amendment Act, 1971, protected laws giving effect to which Directive Principles from being challenged as violating Articles 14 and 19?
o: All Directive Principles in Part IV
advanced.e: Article 31C, as originally inserted by the 25th Amendment Act, 1971, provided that laws implementing the principles in Article 39(b) and (c) would not be void merely for being inconsistent with Articles 14 or 19.

advanced.q: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 amended Article 31C to extend its protective umbrella to?
o: All the Directive Principles contained in Part IV
advanced.e: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 widened Article 31C to protect laws giving effect to any of the Directive Principles in Part IV from challenge under Articles 14 and 19, giving DPSPs sweeping primacy over these Fundamental Rights.

advanced.q: In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court struck down which change made by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976?
o: The insertion of Fundamental Duties under Article 51A
The extension of Article 31C to cover all Directive Principles instead of only Article 39(b) and (c)
The addition of Article 48A on environmental protection
advanced.e: In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court struck down the amendment to Article 31C that extended its protection to all DPSPs, holding that such unlimited primacy of DPSPs over Fundamental Rights (Articles 14 and 19) destroyed the basic structure of the Constitution.

advanced.q: The Minerva Mills case (1980) held that which of the following forms part of the 'basic structure' of the Constitution?
o: Absolute primacy of Directive Principles over Fundamental Rights
The harmonious balance between Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles (Part IV)
Unlimited amending power of Parliament under Article 368
advanced.e: The Supreme Court in Minerva Mills (1980) held that the harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is itself part of the basic structure of the Constitution, and giving absolute primacy to either would upset this balance.

advanced.q: Who was the Chief Justice of India who delivered the leading judgment in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)?
advanced.e: Chief Justice Y.V. Chandrachud delivered the leading judgment in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), holding portions of the 42nd Amendment relating to Article 31C and Article 368 to be unconstitutional.

advanced.q: In Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981), the Supreme Court held that the basic structure doctrine, as propounded in Kesavananda Bharati, would apply?
o: Prospectively, i.e., to constitutional amendments made after 24 April 1973
Only to amendments relating to Directive Principles
Only to amendments relating to the Ninth Schedule enacted before 1951
advanced.e: In Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981), the Supreme Court held that the basic structure doctrine would apply prospectively, i.e., to constitutional amendments enacted after the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment (24 April 1973).

advanced.q: In Unni Krishnan, J.P. v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993), the Supreme Court held that the right to education up to the age of 14 years is a Fundamental Right, deriving it from?
o: Article 21 read with Articles 41 and 45 of the DPSP
advanced.e: In Unni Krishnan v. State of A.P. (1993), the Supreme Court held that the right to education for children up to 14 years flows from the right to life under Article 21, read in light of the directive principles in Articles 41 and 45; this was later made an explicit Fundamental Right under Article 21A by the 86th Amendment.

advanced.q: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 is significant in the DPSP-Fundamental Rights debate because it?
o: Made all DPSPs directly enforceable in courts
Abolished the right to property as a Fundamental Right, converting it into a legal right under Article 300A
Struck down the basic structure doctrine
Reinstated the unlimited primacy of DPSPs over Fundamental Rights
advanced.e: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 removed the right to property from Part III of the Constitution and made it a legal right under Article 300A, easing the tension between DPSPs on distribution of resources and Fundamental Rights.

advanced.q: In Sanjeev Coke Manufacturing Co. v. Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. (1983), the Supreme Court?
o: Upheld the validity of Article 31C as it stood after the Minerva Mills judgment, i.e., limited to Article 39(b) and (c)
Held that Directive Principles are directly enforceable in courts
advanced.e: In Sanjeev Coke Manufacturing Co. v. Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. (1983), the Supreme Court upheld the validity of Article 31C in its original, limited form (protecting laws under Article 39(b) and (c) only), as restored after the Minerva Mills ruling.

advanced.q: Which of the following correctly represents the chronological order of these landmark developments?
o: Kesavananda Bharati - Golaknath - Minerva Mills - Champakam Dorairajan
Champakam Dorairajan - Golaknath - Kesavananda Bharati - Minerva Mills
Minerva Mills - Kesavananda Bharati - Golaknath - Champakam Dorairajan
Golaknath - Champakam Dorairajan - Minerva Mills - Kesavananda Bharati
advanced.e: The correct chronological order is Champakam Dorairajan (1951), followed by Golaknath (1967), then Kesavananda Bharati (1973), and finally Minerva Mills (1980).

advanced.q: The doctrine of 'harmonious construction' between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles, as reaffirmed by the Supreme Court, essentially means that?
o: Directive Principles must always be ignored in favour of Fundamental Rights
Courts should interpret the two Parts so as to give effect to both as far as possible, without either being rendered subordinate to the other in absolute terms
Fundamental Rights are subordinate to Directive Principles in all cases
Only Parliament, and not the judiciary, can decide the relationship between the two Parts
advanced.e: The doctrine of harmonious construction, reaffirmed in cases like Minerva Mills, requires that Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles be interpreted together in a balanced manner, so that the object of both Parts III and IV of the Constitution is achieved.

basic.q: In which Part of the Indian Constitution are the Fundamental Duties enshrined?
basic.e: The Fundamental Duties are contained in Part IVA of the Constitution, which consists of a single Article, 51A.

basic.q: Which Article of the Constitution lists the Fundamental Duties of citizens?
basic.e: Article 51A enumerates the Fundamental Duties of every citizen of India.

basic.q: The Fundamental Duties were added to the Constitution by which Amendment Act?
basic.e: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 inserted Part IVA containing Article 51A, listing the Fundamental Duties.

basic.q: The incorporation of Fundamental Duties into the Constitution was based on the recommendations of which committee?
basic.e: The Swaran Singh Committee (1976) recommended a separate chapter on Fundamental Duties, leading to their addition through the 42nd Amendment.

basic.q: How many Fundamental Duties were originally incorporated by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976?
basic.e: Originally, ten Fundamental Duties, covering clauses (a) to (j), were added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.

basic.q: The 11th Fundamental Duty was added by which Amendment Act?
basic.e: The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 inserted clause (k) into Article 51A, adding the 11th Fundamental Duty.

basic.q: The 11th Fundamental Duty added in 2002 casts an obligation on whom?
o: Parents or guardians to provide education to their child or ward
The State to provide free education
basic.e: Clause (k) obliges a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to his/her child or ward between the ages of six and fourteen years.

basic.q: The concept of Fundamental Duties in the Indian Constitution draws inspiration from the constitution of which country?
basic.e: The idea of Fundamental Duties was inspired by the Constitution of the erstwhile USSR.

basic.q: Which of the following best describes the legal character of Fundamental Duties?
basic.e: Like the Directive Principles of State Policy, Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable; there is no direct constitutional sanction for their violation.

basic.q: Which committee, appointed in 1999, examined ways of operationalising the Fundamental Duties?
o: National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution
basic.e: The Justice J.S. Verma Committee (1999) was constituted to suggest ways to operationalise the Fundamental Duties.

basic.q: Fundamental Duties under Article 51A are applicable to:
basic.e: Article 51A applies only to every citizen of India and does not extend to foreigners residing in India.

basic.q: Along with the 11th Fundamental Duty, the 86th Amendment Act, 2002 also inserted which new Article guaranteeing a right to education?
basic.e: The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A, making free and compulsory education a Fundamental Right for children aged six to fourteen years, alongside the corresponding 11th Fundamental Duty.

basic.q: In which year was the 42nd Constitutional Amendment, which introduced Fundamental Duties, enacted?
basic.e: The 42nd Amendment Act was enacted in 1976, adding Part IVA with the Fundamental Duties.

basic.q: In which year was the 86th Constitutional Amendment, which added the 11th Fundamental Duty, enacted?
basic.e: The 86th Amendment Act was enacted in 2002, adding clause (k) to Article 51A.

basic.q: As of now, how many Fundamental Duties are listed under Article 51A?
basic.e: There are currently eleven Fundamental Duties, clauses (a) to (k), following the addition of clause (k) by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about Fundamental Duties: 1. They were added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976. 2. They are enforceable in a court of law like Fundamental Rights. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Statement 1 is correct; statement 2 is incorrect since Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable and cannot be directly enforced through courts.

intermediate.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the Fundamental Duties enumerated in Article 51A?
o: To safeguard public property and abjure violence
To develop scientific temper and spirit of inquiry
To protect and improve the natural environment
intermediate.e: Paying taxes is not among the eleven Fundamental Duties; the other three options correspond to clauses (i), (h) and (g) of Article 51A respectively.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements: 1. The Swaran Singh Committee recommended that Parliament may provide for imposition of penalties for non-compliance with Fundamental Duties. 2. This recommendation was fully incorporated into Article 51A. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The Swaran Singh Committee did recommend a penal provision, but this was not accepted by the government, and no such penalty clause exists in Article 51A.

intermediate.q: Which of the following pairs of Fundamental Duty and its clause under Article 51A is correctly matched?
o: Clause (e) - to safeguard public property and abjure violence
Clause (g) - to protect and improve the natural environment
intermediate.e: Clause (g) of Article 51A casts the duty to protect and improve the natural environment, including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife, and to have compassion for living creatures.

intermediate.q: Which of the following is a Fundamental Duty of an Indian citizen under Article 51A?
o: To cherish and follow the noble ideals which inspired the national struggle for freedom
intermediate.e: Clause (b) of Article 51A requires citizens to cherish and follow the noble ideals which inspired the national struggle for freedom.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements regarding the 11th Fundamental Duty: 1. It was added by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002. 2. It requires every citizen to educate children between ages six and fourteen. 3. It specifically applies to a parent or guardian of the child or ward. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Statement 2 is incorrect because the duty applies specifically to the parent or guardian, not every citizen in general; statements 1 and 3 are correct.

intermediate.q: Which of the following statements about Fundamental Duties is correct?
o: They can be enforced directly by courts through writs
Some duties may be indirectly enforced through existing laws, such as the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971
They apply equally to citizens and foreigners
They were part of the original Constitution of 1950
intermediate.e: Although Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable, certain duties can be indirectly enforced through ordinary legislation such as the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements: 1. Fundamental Duties are contained in Part IVA of the Constitution. 2. Directive Principles of State Policy are contained in Part IV of the Constitution. 3. Fundamental Rights are contained in Part III of the Constitution. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: All three statements are accurate: Part III covers Fundamental Rights, Part IV covers Directive Principles, and Part IVA covers Fundamental Duties.

intermediate.q: Which of the following duties relates to promoting harmony among the people of India under Article 51A?
intermediate.e: Clause (e) of Article 51A enjoins citizens to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood amongst all people of India, transcending religious, linguistic, regional or sectional diversities.

intermediate.q: Which of the following is NOT a correct match of Fundamental Duty clause with its content?
o: Clause (a) - respect the Constitution, National Flag and National Anthem
Clause (c) - uphold and protect sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
Clause (j) - strive towards excellence in all spheres of activity
Clause (h) - defend the country and render national service
intermediate.e: Defending the country and rendering national service is clause (d), not clause (h); clause (h) actually deals with developing scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about the applicability of Fundamental Duties: 1. They are binding only on citizens of India. 2. Foreign nationals residing in India are also bound by Article 51A. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Article 51A addresses every citizen of India, and hence it does not extend its obligations to foreign nationals.

intermediate.q: Which of the following duties under Article 51A pertains to India's composite culture?
o: To value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture
To uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
To develop the scientific temper and spirit of inquiry
intermediate.e: Clause (f) of Article 51A requires citizens to value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements: 1. The Fundamental Duties, unlike Fundamental Rights, are confined to citizens only. 2. Some Fundamental Rights, such as those under Articles 14 and 21, are available to non-citizens too. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Both statements are correct; unlike certain Fundamental Rights (e.g., Articles 14 and 21) available to all persons, Fundamental Duties apply only to citizens.

intermediate.q: Which of the following is a Fundamental Duty relating to public property?
o: To safeguard public property and to abjure violence
To pay taxes for public infrastructure
intermediate.e: Clause (i) of Article 51A obliges citizens to safeguard public property and to abjure violence.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about the Justice Verma Committee (1999): 1. It was constituted to suggest methods for operationalising the Fundamental Duties. 2. It recommended a new set of Fundamental Duties in addition to the existing eleven. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The Justice Verma Committee focused on ways to operationalise the existing Fundamental Duties through education, awareness and legal remedies, rather than proposing new duties.

advanced.q: Which of the following recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee regarding Fundamental Duties was NOT accepted by Parliament while enacting the 42nd Amendment?
o: Inclusion of a separate chapter on Fundamental Duties
Empowering Parliament to provide penalties for non-compliance with Fundamental Duties
Placing the Fundamental Duties after the Directive Principles
advanced.e: The Committee's suggestion that Parliament be authorised to impose penalties for non-compliance with Fundamental Duties was not incorporated into the final text of Article 51A.

advanced.q: Which statement best captures the constitutional status of Fundamental Duties relative to Fundamental Rights?
o: Both are equally justiciable and enforceable by writ petitions
Fundamental Duties are justiciable but Fundamental Rights are not
Fundamental Rights are justiciable while Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable moral and civic obligations
Neither Fundamental Rights nor Fundamental Duties are enforceable
advanced.e: Fundamental Rights (Part III) are legally enforceable through courts, whereas Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) are non-justiciable and function as moral and civic obligations.

advanced.q: The Supreme Court has used Fundamental Duties in judicial interpretation primarily to:
o: Strike down laws inconsistent with Fundamental Duties
Interpret the reasonableness of restrictions on Fundamental Rights and uphold the validity of laws promoting duties
Directly penalise citizens who violate Article 51A
Amend the Constitution without a formal amendment process
advanced.e: Courts have often invoked Fundamental Duties to assess the reasonableness of restrictions on Fundamental Rights and to judge the constitutional validity of laws giving effect to those duties, even though the duties are not directly enforceable.

advanced.q: Which of the following statements about the original ten Fundamental Duties (1976) versus the current eleven is correct?
o: All eleven duties were part of the original 42nd Amendment
The 42nd Amendment added clauses (a) to (j); the 86th Amendment added clause (k)
The Swaran Singh Committee recommended eleven duties which were all adopted at once
advanced.e: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 introduced clauses (a) to (j); clause (k), the 11th duty, was added later by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002.

advanced.q: Which of the following is the most accurate reason why Fundamental Duties are considered non-justiciable?
o: The Constitution explicitly bars courts from interpreting Article 51A
No mechanism or sanction has been prescribed in the Constitution for their direct enforcement against a defaulting citizen
They apply only to a small section of citizens
They are located in Part III of the Constitution
advanced.e: The Constitution does not prescribe any direct legal sanction or mechanism for enforcing Article 51A duties against individuals, distinguishing them from Fundamental Rights.

advanced.q: Consider the following statements: 1. Article 51A(g) casts a duty to protect the environment and is often read alongside Article 48A, a Directive Principle on environmental protection. 2. Article 51A(k) is linked with Article 21A, a Fundamental Right on education. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
advanced.e: Both linkages are well recognised: clause (g) parallels the Directive Principle in Article 48A on environment protection, and clause (k) parallels the Fundamental Right in Article 21A on education.

advanced.q: Which of the following was a recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee that WAS eventually accepted?
o: A penal provision for violation of duties
Insertion of a new chapter, Part IVA, on Fundamental Duties in the Constitution
advanced.e: The Committee's core recommendation to add a distinct chapter enumerating Fundamental Duties was accepted and implemented as Part IVA via the 42nd Amendment.

advanced.q: Which of the following statements regarding comparison of Fundamental Duties with Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) is correct?
o: Both are non-justiciable, but Fundamental Duties bind citizens while DPSPs are addressed to the State
DPSPs bind citizens while Fundamental Duties bind the State
Both are enumerated in Part III
advanced.e: Fundamental Duties and DPSPs are both non-justiciable, but Fundamental Duties are obligations of citizens, whereas Directive Principles (Part IV) are directions to the State.

advanced.q: Which of the following duties under Article 51A most directly reflects the ideal of scientific temper and rationalism?
advanced.e: Clause (h) of Article 51A obliges citizens to develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform.

advanced.q: In the case of an alleged conflict between a citizen's Fundamental Right and a corresponding Fundamental Duty, which is the accepted constitutional position?
o: The Fundamental Duty automatically overrides the Fundamental Right
The Fundamental Right remains enforceable and the corresponding duty serves only as a moral reminder unless separate legislation gives it legal force
Courts must strike down the exercise of the Fundamental Right
The matter must be referred to the President for adjudication
advanced.e: Since Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable, a Fundamental Right continues to be enforceable unless a duly enacted law reasonably restricts it; the duty by itself has only moral force.

advanced.q: Which of the following statements about the 86th Amendment Act, 2002 is correct?
o: It added only the 11th Fundamental Duty and made no other constitutional changes
It added Article 21A, amended Article 45, and inserted the 11th Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(k)
It replaced the Directive Principle on education with a Fundamental Duty
advanced.e: The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 made three linked changes: inserting Article 21A (Right to Education), amending Article 45 (early childhood care), and adding the 11th Fundamental Duty, clause (k).

advanced.q: Which of the following best explains why Fundamental Duties were NOT included in the original Constitution of 1950 but added later in 1976?
o: The Constituent Assembly rejected the idea outright and permanently

The framers considered them unnecessary since Fundamental Rights sufficed, and the felt need for a separate chapter arose later, following the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendations during the Emergency period
Fundamental Duties were mandated by an international treaty ratified in 1975
The Supreme Court directed their inclusion in the Kesavananda Bharati case
advanced.e: Fundamental Duties were absent in the original 1950 Constitution; the idea gained momentum later, and on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee, they were incorporated during the Emergency period via the 42nd Amendment.

advanced.q: Which of the following statements about enforceability of Fundamental Duties through ordinary law is correct?
o: No law in India gives any effect to Fundamental Duties
The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 indirectly supports the duty to respect the National Flag and Anthem under Article 51A(a)
Parliament is constitutionally barred from legislating on subjects covered by Fundamental Duties
Fundamental Duties can only be enforced through a Presidential ordinance
advanced.e: The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 penalises disrespect to the Constitution, National Flag, and National Anthem, thereby indirectly reinforcing the duty under Article 51A(a).

advanced.q: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched with respect to Article 51A?
o: Clause (c) - uphold and protect sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
Clause (j) - strive towards excellence in individual and collective activity
Clause (k) - added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976
Clause (g) - protect and improve the natural environment
advanced.e: Clause (k) was added by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002, not the 42nd Amendment Act; the other three pairs are correctly matched.

advanced.q: With reference to Fundamental Duties, consider the following statements: 1. The Justice Verma Committee (1999) suggested using the existing legal framework to give teeth to certain Fundamental Duties rather than proposing wholly new punitive laws. 2. Its recommendations led to a constitutional amendment prescribing penalties for violation of all eleven Fundamental Duties. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
advanced.e: The Justice Verma Committee emphasised using existing laws and administrative/educational measures to operationalise duties; no constitutional amendment has since prescribed blanket penalties for violating all Fundamental Duties.

title: Amendment of the Constitution
desc: Article 368, amendment procedures, and key amendments

basic.q: Which Part of the Constitution contains Article 368, which deals with the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution?
basic.e: Article 368 is located in Part XX of the Constitution, titled 'Amendment of the Constitution'.

basic.q: The title of Part XX of the Constitution, which contains Article 368, is:
basic.e: Part XX is titled 'Amendment of the Constitution' and contains only Article 368.

basic.q: How many distinct procedures does the Indian Constitution provide for its amendment?
basic.e: The Constitution can be amended in three ways: by simple majority, by special majority under Article 368, and by special majority with ratification by states.

basic.q: Which of the following can be amended by a simple majority of Parliament, as in ordinary law-making, without invoking Article 368?
o: Distribution of legislative powers between Union and States
basic.e: Formation of new states and alteration of boundaries under Articles 2-4 are done by simple majority, outside the scope of Article 368.

basic.q: What is the 'special majority' required under Article 368 for most constitutional amendments?
o: Simple majority of members present and voting
Majority of total membership of each House and two-thirds majority of members present and voting
Two-thirds of total membership of each House
Three-fourths majority of members present and voting
basic.e: Special majority under Article 368 means a majority of the total membership of each House and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting.

basic.q: Which Schedule was inserted into the Constitution by the First Amendment Act, 1951?
basic.e: The First Amendment Act, 1951 inserted the Ninth Schedule along with Articles 31A and 31B to protect land reform laws from judicial review.

basic.q: The Seventh Amendment Act, 1956 was enacted to give effect to which reorganization?
o: Linguistic reorganization under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956
basic.e: The 7th Amendment Act, 1956 implemented the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, abolishing the four-fold classification of states into Part A, B, C and D.

basic.q: Which amendment is popularly known as the 'Mini-Constitution'?
basic.e: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 made sweeping changes and is popularly called the 'Mini-Constitution'.

basic.q: The words 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added to the Preamble by which amendment?
basic.e: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 added the words 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' to the Preamble.

basic.q: Fundamental Duties were added to the Constitution under which Article by the 42nd Amendment?
basic.e: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 inserted Article 51A in a new Part IVA, laying down Fundamental Duties.

basic.q: Which amendment changed the ground for declaring a National Emergency from 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion'?
basic.e: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' as a ground for National Emergency under Article 352.

basic.q: The Right to Property ceased to be a Fundamental Right and became a legal right under which Article, following the 44th Amendment?
basic.e: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 deleted the Right to Property from Part III and made it a legal right under Article 300A.

basic.q: The 73rd Amendment Act, 1992 deals with which subject?
basic.e: The 73rd Amendment Act, 1992 gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj institutions through Part IX.

basic.q: The 74th Amendment Act, 1992 introduced constitutional provisions for:
basic.e: The 74th Amendment Act, 1992 added Part IXA on Municipalities, providing them constitutional status.

basic.q: Which amendment inserted Article 21A, guaranteeing the Right to Education as a Fundamental Right?
basic.e: The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A, making free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14 a Fundamental Right.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about the amendment procedure under Article 368: 1. It requires a special majority in each House of Parliament. 2. It requires ratification by all state legislatures for every amendment. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Only some amendments (those in the proviso to Article 368(2)) require ratification by not less than one-half of state legislatures; it is not required for every amendment.

intermediate.q: Which of the following requires ratification by state legislatures in addition to a special majority in Parliament?
o: Creation of Legislative Councils in states
Manner of election of the President
Second Schedule salaries of the Speaker
intermediate.e: The manner of election of the President (Articles 54 and 55) is among the provisions listed in the proviso to Article 368(2) requiring ratification by half the states.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements regarding the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976: 1. It added the Fundamental Duties. 2. It added the words 'Socialist' and 'Secular' to the Preamble. 3. It curtailed the scope of judicial review. How many of the above statements are correct?
intermediate.e: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 added Fundamental Duties, inserted 'Socialist' and 'Secular' into the Preamble, and curtailed judicial review by amending Articles 368 and 31C.

intermediate.q: Which amendment introduced the Goods and Services Tax (GST) regime in India?
intermediate.e: The 101st Amendment Act, 2016 introduced the Goods and Services Tax (GST) by inserting Articles 246A, 269A and 279A.

intermediate.q: The 103rd Amendment Act, 2019 provides for reservation of what percentage of seats/posts for Economically Weaker Sections?
intermediate.e: The 103rd Amendment Act, 2019 added Articles 15(6) and 16(6), providing 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS).

intermediate.q: Granville Austin described the amending process of the Indian Constitution as:
o: A synthesis of rigidity and flexibility
intermediate.e: Granville Austin described the Indian Constitution's amending process as a 'synthesis of rigidity and flexibility', combining elements of rigid constitutions like the USA and flexible ones like the UK.

intermediate.q: Which of the following is amended by simple majority, not requiring the special procedure under Article 368?
o: Salaries and allowances of the President under the Second Schedule
Extent of executive power of states
intermediate.e: Salaries, allowances and privileges under the Second Schedule can be altered by simple majority, as an ordinary legislative matter outside Article 368.

intermediate.q: For an amendment requiring ratification by state legislatures, what proportion of states must ratify the amendment?
o: Not less than one-half of the states
Not less than two-thirds of the states
Not less than one-third of the states
intermediate.e: As per the proviso to Article 368(2), ratification requires resolutions passed by not less than one-half of the state legislatures.

intermediate.q: By what majority must a state legislature pass a resolution to ratify a constitutional amendment?
intermediate.e: State legislatures ratify amendments by a simple majority resolution; no special majority is prescribed for ratification by states.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about the 1st Amendment Act, 1951: 1. It added the Ninth Schedule. 2. It inserted Articles 31A and 31B. 3. It added new grounds of restriction to freedom of speech under Article 19(2). Which of the statements given above are correct?
intermediate.e: The 1st Amendment Act, 1951 added the Ninth Schedule, inserted Articles 31A and 31B, and added grounds like public order and friendly relations with foreign states to Article 19(2).

intermediate.q: Match the following amendments with their subject matter: (1) 7th Amendment (2) 73rd Amendment (3) 86th Amendment (4) 101st Amendment; with (a) GST (b) Right to Education (c) States Reorganisation (d) Panchayati Raj
intermediate.e: The 7th Amendment relates to States Reorganisation, the 73rd to Panchayati Raj, the 86th to Right to Education, and the 101st to GST.

intermediate.q: Which of the following amendments does NOT require ratification by state legislatures?
o: Amendment altering distribution of legislative powers between Union and States
Amendment to provisions on election of the President
intermediate.e: Addition of Fundamental Duties under Article 51A (via the 42nd Amendment) required only a special majority of Parliament, not state ratification, as it is not listed in the proviso to Article 368(2).

intermediate.q: The abolition of Legislative Councils in states is done through:
o: A Constitutional Amendment Act under Article 368 with state ratification
An ordinary law of Parliament passed by simple majority under Article 169
A resolution of the Rajya Sabha alone
intermediate.e: Under Article 169, Parliament can create or abolish Legislative Councils by an ordinary law passed by simple majority, after the state assembly passes a special resolution.

intermediate.q: In a rigid constitution like that of the USA, amendment typically requires:
o: A simple majority of the legislature
A special and often more elaborate procedure distinct from ordinary law-making
intermediate.e: Rigid constitutions, such as the USA's, require a special, more difficult amending procedure than ordinary lawmaking, unlike flexible constitutions such as the UK's.

intermediate.q: Which of the following best describes a 'flexible' constitution such as that of the United Kingdom?
o: It can be amended by the same procedure as ordinary laws
It cannot be amended at all
It requires a national referendum for every amendment
It requires ratification by all constituent units
intermediate.e: A flexible constitution, like the UK's unwritten constitution, can be amended by the same procedure used for ordinary legislation.

advanced.q: Which of the following can be altered by Parliament through simple majority, even though it relates to the judiciary?
o: Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 138
Appointment procedure for Supreme Court judges under Article 124
Provisions relating to High Courts under Chapter V of Part VI
advanced.e: Under Article 138, Parliament may confer additional jurisdiction on the Supreme Court by an ordinary law passed with a simple majority, without invoking Article 368.

advanced.q: The power of Parliament to regulate citizenship under Article 11 is exercised by:
advanced.e: Article 11 empowers Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law, passed by a simple majority, outside the scope of Article 368.

advanced.q: Which landmark case held that Parliament's constituent power under Article 368 cannot be used to alter the 'basic structure' of the Constitution?
o: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)
Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951)
advanced.e: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the Supreme Court held that Parliament's amending power under Article 368 does not extend to damaging or destroying the 'basic structure' of the Constitution.

advanced.q: Which amendment made it obligatory for the President to give assent to a Constitution Amendment Bill passed under Article 368?
advanced.e: The 24th Amendment Act, 1971 made it obligatory for the President to give assent to any Constitution Amendment Bill, reversing the discretion previously assumed to exist.

advanced.q: The 24th Amendment Act, 1971 was enacted primarily in response to which Supreme Court judgment?
o: Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain case
advanced.e: The 24th Amendment Act, 1971 was enacted to overcome the Golaknath (1967) ruling, which had held that Parliament could not amend Fundamental Rights under Article 368.

advanced.q: The 42nd Amendment Act's attempt to place constitutional amendments beyond judicial review (by adding clauses 4 and 5 to Article 368) was:
o: Upheld in full by the Supreme Court
Struck down in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)
advanced.e: In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court struck down clauses 4 and 5 added to Article 368 by the 42nd Amendment, holding that judicial review is part of the basic structure.

advanced.q: Why is the Indian Constitution often described as 'neither too rigid nor too flexible'?
o: Because it can only be amended by a national referendum
Because it provides different procedures of varying difficulty for different provisions
Because Article 368 is the sole method of amendment for all provisions
Because only the judiciary can amend it
advanced.e: The Constitution provides three different procedures of varying stringency-simple majority, special majority, and special majority with state ratification-making it a blend of rigidity and flexibility.

advanced.q: Consider the following statements: 1. All amendments to the Seventh Schedule require ratification by states. 2. Amendments relating to the Union List alone can be made by simple majority. Which is correct?
advanced.e: Any amendment relating to any of the lists in the Seventh Schedule (Union, State, or Concurrent) falls under the proviso to Article 368(2) and requires ratification by states, not simple majority.

advanced.q: Which of the following changes was NOT made by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978?
o: Deletion of the Right to Property as a Fundamental Right
Change of 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion' for National Emergency
Addition of the words 'Socialist' and 'Secular' to the Preamble
Restoration of the five-year term for Lok Sabha and State Assemblies
advanced.e: The words 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment, not the 44th Amendment, which largely reversed the 42nd Amendment's excesses.

advanced.q: The provision for extension of the term of the Lok Sabha from five to six years during an emergency, introduced by the 42nd Amendment, was:
o: Reversed by the 44th Amendment, restoring the five-year term
advanced.e: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 restored the normal term of the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies to five years, reversing the 42nd Amendment's extension to six years.

advanced.q: Under the proviso to Article 368(2), which of the following is included among matters requiring state ratification?
advanced.e: Representation of states in Parliament is among the entrenched provisions listed in the proviso to Article 368(2) requiring ratification by half the states.

advanced.q: Which of these statements about the amendment procedure is correct? 1. A Constitution Amendment Bill can be introduced in either House of Parliament. 2. There is no provision for a joint sitting of both Houses to resolve a deadlock over a Constitution Amendment Bill.
advanced.e: A Constitution Amendment Bill may be introduced in either House, and unlike ordinary bills, there is no provision for a joint sitting under Article 368 to resolve disagreements between the Houses.

advanced.q: The distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States, if amended, requires:
o: Special majority of Parliament plus ratification by half the states
advanced.e: Amendments affecting the distribution of legislative powers (Chapter I of Part XI) require special majority plus ratification by not less than half the state legislatures, as per the proviso to Article 368(2).

advanced.q: Which of the following is an example of an amendment passed by simple majority rather than under Article 368?
o: Admission or establishment of new states under Articles 2 and 3
Amendment of Fundamental Rights in Part III
Amendment altering the powers of the Supreme Court
Amendment to Article 54 on Presidential election
advanced.e: Under Articles 2 and 3, Parliament can admit or establish new states by an ordinary law passed with simple majority, without following the Article 368 procedure.

advanced.q: The Indian Constitution's amending procedure has been described as combining features of which two types of constitutions?
o: Rigid constitutions like the USA's and flexible constitutions like the UK's
advanced.e: India's amending procedure blends features of rigid constitutions (like the USA, needing special procedures) and flexible constitutions (like the UK's, amendable by ordinary process), making it a unique synthesis.

title: Basic Structure Doctrine
desc: Origin, evolution and key cases shaping it

basic.q: The Basic Structure Doctrine was propounded by the Supreme Court in which landmark case?
o: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Minerva Mills v. Union of India
Shankari Prasad v. Union of India
basic.e: The Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) case originated the Basic Structure Doctrine, holding that Parliament's amending power under Article 368 does not extend to altering the basic structure of the Constitution.

basic.q: The Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) was decided by a Supreme Court bench of how many judges?
basic.e: Kesavananda Bharati was heard by a 13-judge bench, the largest ever constituted by the Supreme Court of India.

basic.q: By what margin was the Kesavananda Bharati judgment (1973) delivered?
basic.e: The Kesavananda Bharati verdict was delivered by a thin majority of 7:6, making it one of the most closely contested judgments in Indian constitutional history.

basic.q: The Kesavananda Bharati judgment (1973) overruled the Supreme Court's earlier decision in which case?
basic.e: Kesavananda Bharati overruled the Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967) ruling, which had held that Fundamental Rights could not be amended at all.

basic.q: The Golaknath v. State of Punjab case was decided in which year?
basic.e: The Golaknath case was decided in 1967, holding that Parliament had no power to amend Fundamental Rights.

basic.q: The Golaknath case (1967) was decided by what majority?
basic.e: The Golaknath judgment was delivered by an 11-judge bench with a majority of 6:5, holding Fundamental Rights to be beyond the amending power of Parliament.

basic.q: Which doctrine, borrowed from American constitutional law, was applied by the Supreme Court in the Golaknath case?
basic.e: In Golaknath, the Court applied the doctrine of prospective overruling, meaning the ruling would apply only to future amendments, leaving past constitutional amendments undisturbed.

basic.q: Which Constitutional Amendment Act was enacted specifically to overcome the effect of the Golaknath judgment?
basic.e: The 24th Amendment Act, 1971 was enacted to nullify the effect of the Golaknath ruling by affirming Parliament's power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights.

basic.q: The 24th Amendment Act, 1971 made it obligatory for whom to give assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill?
basic.e: The 24th Amendment Act made it obligatory for the President to give assent to any Constitutional Amendment Bill passed by Parliament, removing prior discretion in this regard.

basic.q: In the Shankari Prasad case (1951), the Supreme Court held that Parliament's power under Article 368 includes the power to amend which part of the Constitution?
basic.e: In Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951), the Supreme Court held that Parliament's power to amend under Article 368 includes the power to amend Fundamental Rights as well.

basic.q: The Sajjan Singh case, which upheld the view taken in the Shankari Prasad case, was decided in which year?
basic.e: The Sajjan Singh case (1965) reaffirmed the position taken in Shankari Prasad, that Parliament could amend Fundamental Rights under Article 368.

basic.q: In which case did the Supreme Court apply the Basic Structure Doctrine to strike down a provision placing election disputes of the Prime Minister beyond judicial scrutiny?
o: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain
basic.e: In Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), the Supreme Court struck down a provision that sought to place the Prime Minister's election dispute outside judicial review, holding free and fair elections and judicial review to be part of the basic structure.

basic.q: Which Constitutional Amendment inserted clause 4 into Article 329A, which was struck down in the Indira Gandhi election case?
basic.e: The 39th Amendment Act inserted Article 329A, clause 4 of which sought to keep the Prime Minister's and Speaker's election disputes outside judicial review; this clause was struck down as violative of the basic structure.

basic.q: The Minerva Mills v. Union of India case, in which unlimited amending power granted to Parliament was struck down, was decided in which year?
basic.e: Minerva Mills v. Union of India was decided in 1980, striking down provisions of the 42nd Amendment that gave Parliament unlimited amending power.

basic.q: Which case held that the Basic Structure Doctrine applies to constitutional amendments enacted after 24 April 1973?
basic.e: In the Waman Rao case (1981), the Supreme Court held that the basic structure doctrine would apply prospectively to constitutional amendments made after 24 April 1973, the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment.

intermediate.q: Consider the following cases: 1. Golaknath v. State of Punjab 2. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala 3. Shankari Prasad v. Union of India 4. Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain. What is the correct chronological order of these cases?
intermediate.e: The correct chronological order is Shankari Prasad (1951) -> Golaknath (1967) -> Kesavananda Bharati (1973) -> Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), tracing the doctrine's evolution.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements regarding the Shankari Prasad and Golaknath cases: 1. Both cases dealt with the amendability of Fundamental Rights under Article 368. 2. Golaknath reversed the position taken earlier in Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Both statements are correct: Shankari Prasad, Sajjan Singh and Golaknath all concerned amendability of Fundamental Rights, and Golaknath (1967) reversed the earlier pro-amendment view of Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965), holding Fundamental Rights unamendable.

intermediate.q: With reference to the Minerva Mills case (1980), consider the following statements: 1. It struck down clauses (4) and (5) added to Article 368 by the 42nd Amendment. 2. It struck down the widened version of Article 31C introduced by the 42nd Amendment. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: In Minerva Mills, the Supreme Court struck down both the amendments to Article 368 clauses (4) and (5) (which gave Parliament unlimited amending power) and the amendment to Article 31C (which gave DPSPs absolute primacy over Articles 14 and 19).

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about the 24th Amendment Act, 1971: 1. It was enacted in response to the Golaknath judgment. 2. It made presidential assent to constitutional amendment bills obligatory. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The 24th Amendment Act, 1971 was passed to overcome the Golaknath ruling and affirmed Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights; it also made it obligatory for the President to give assent to constitutional amendment bills.

intermediate.q: With reference to the Kesavananda Bharati judgment (1973), consider the following statements: 1. It held that Parliament has power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights. 2. It held that this amending power does not extend to altering the basic structure of the Constitution. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Kesavananda Bharati struck a middle path: it upheld Parliament's power to amend any part, including Fundamental Rights (overruling Golaknath's absolute bar), but held this power was subject to the limitation that the basic structure could not be altered.

intermediate.q: The Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain case is directly linked to a challenge against which constitutional provision?
intermediate.e: The case arose from a challenge to Article 329A, inserted by the 39th Amendment, clause 4 of which sought to immunize the Prime Minister's election dispute from judicial review.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements: 1. The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 inserted clauses (4) and (5) into Article 368. 2. These clauses were struck down by the Supreme Court in the Minerva Mills case. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 added clauses (4) and (5) to Article 368 to give Parliament unlimited constituent power beyond judicial review; these were struck down in Minerva Mills (1980) as destructive of the basic structure.

intermediate.q: The I.R. Coelho case (2007) primarily dealt with judicial review of which category of laws?
o: Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973
intermediate.e: In I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), the Supreme Court held that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are open to judicial review if they violate the basic structure or Fundamental Rights.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements regarding elements of the basic structure of the Constitution: 1. Judicial review has been held to be part of the basic structure. 2. Federal character of the Constitution has been held to be part of the basic structure. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Through various judgments, the Supreme Court has recognised judicial review and the federal character of the Constitution, among other features, as part of the basic structure.

intermediate.q: The significance of 24 April 1973 in the context of the Waman Rao case lies in the fact that it is the date of which event?
o: Pronouncement of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment
intermediate.e: 24 April 1973 is the date on which the Kesavananda Bharati judgment was pronounced; the Waman Rao case used this date as the cut-off for prospective application of the basic structure doctrine.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about the Minerva Mills case (1980): 1. It held that a total absence of judicial review would be destructive of the basic structure. 2. It emphasised the balance and harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles as part of the basic structure. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Minerva Mills held that judicial review is a basic feature, and that the harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSP is also part of the basic structure of the Constitution.

intermediate.q: The term "basic structure" is generally traced to have first found judicial mention in which context, prior to Kesavananda Bharati?
o: Justice Mudholkar's dissenting opinion in the Sajjan Singh case
The majority opinion in the Shankari Prasad case
The majority opinion in the Golaknath case
The 24th Amendment's Statement of Objects and Reasons
intermediate.e: Before Kesavananda Bharati, the idea of implied limitations on the amending power was hinted at in Justice Mudholkar's dissenting opinion in the Sajjan Singh case (1965).

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements regarding bench strength in landmark basic structure cases: 1. Golaknath was decided by an 11-judge bench. 2. Kesavananda Bharati was decided by a 13-judge bench. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Golaknath was heard by an 11-judge bench and Kesavananda Bharati, the largest bench ever constituted, by a 13-judge bench.

intermediate.q: In the Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain case, the Supreme Court held that which of the following is/are part of the basic structure? 1. Free and fair elections 2. Judicial review. Select the correct answer using the code below.
intermediate.e: The Court held that both free and fair elections and judicial review constitute part of the basic structure, and hence Article 329A(4) which excluded judicial scrutiny of the PM's election was unconstitutional.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about the features constituting the basic structure of the Constitution: 1. The list of basic features has been exhaustively and finally defined by the Supreme Court. 2. The Supreme Court has added to the list of basic features from case to case. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The Supreme Court has never provided an exhaustive definition of the basic structure; instead, the list of basic features has been expanded and clarified case by case, such as secularism, federalism, rule of law, and separation of powers.

advanced.q: In Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), the Supreme Court specifically struck down which clause of Article 329A?
advanced.e: The Court struck down clause (4) of Article 329A, which sought to validate the Prime Minister's election retrospectively and place it beyond judicial review, as violative of free and fair elections and judicial review, both part of the basic structure.

advanced.q: Which of the following most accurately describes what the Minerva Mills judgment (1980) actually struck down?
o: Only clauses (4) and (5) inserted into Article 368, and the amendment to Article 31C, by the 42nd Amendment
Only the amendment to Article 31C, leaving Article 368 changes intact
The entire Ninth Schedule as inserted by the 42nd Amendment
advanced.e: Minerva Mills did not strike down the entire 42nd Amendment; it struck down only the specific provisions that inserted clauses (4) and (5) into Article 368 and the amendment widening Article 31C, as destructive of the basic structure.

advanced.q: What is the key distinction between the holdings of Golaknath (1967) and Kesavananda Bharati (1973) with respect to Fundamental Rights?
o: Golaknath allowed Fundamental Rights to be amended freely, while Kesavananda Bharati barred it completely
Golaknath held Fundamental Rights were completely unamendable, while Kesavananda Bharati held they could be amended so long as the basic structure is not damaged
Both cases held Fundamental Rights were completely unamendable
Both cases held Fundamental Rights could be amended without any limitation
advanced.e: Golaknath held that Fundamental Rights enjoy a transcendental position and cannot be abridged or amended at all, whereas Kesavananda Bharati overruled this rigidity, holding that Fundamental Rights can be amended as long as the amendment does not damage the basic structure.

advanced.q: Regarding vote margins, which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
advanced.e: Golaknath was decided by a majority of 6:5, while Kesavananda Bharati, decided six years later with two additional judges on the bench, was decided by a majority of 7:6.

advanced.q: Whose dissenting opinion in the Sajjan Singh case (1965) is regarded as an early judicial precursor to the idea of implied limitations on the amending power, later crystallised as the Basic Structure Doctrine?
advanced.e: Justice Mudholkar's dissent in Sajjan Singh raised the question of whether the Constitution possesses certain fundamental features that even a constitutional amendment could not alter, foreshadowing the basic structure doctrine.

advanced.q: As per the ruling in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), what is the precise legal position on laws included in the Ninth Schedule?
o: All laws in the Ninth Schedule, irrespective of date of insertion, are completely immune from judicial review
Laws added to the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are open to judicial review if they violate the basic structure or Fundamental Rights
Laws added to the Ninth Schedule before 24 April 1973 are open to challenge, but those added after are immune
The Ninth Schedule itself was declared unconstitutional
advanced.e: The Coelho judgment clarified that laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda Bharati verdict) can be tested against the basic structure and Fundamental Rights, even though Article 31B otherwise shields Ninth Schedule laws from being challenged as violative of Fundamental Rights.

advanced.q: Which amendment attempted to give Parliament unlimited constituent power exempt from judicial review, and was subsequently struck down for violating the basic structure?
o: 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, inserting clauses (4) and (5) in Article 368
44th Amendment Act, 1978, restoring the right to property as a legal right
advanced.e: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 inserted clauses (4) and (5) into Article 368 declaring that no constitutional amendment could be questioned in any court and that Parliament's amending power was unlimited; this was struck down in Minerva Mills (1980).

advanced.q: Which statement correctly captures the scope of the Minerva Mills verdict on the 42nd Amendment?
o: The Court struck down the 42nd Amendment in its entirety as unconstitutional
The Court upheld the entire 42nd Amendment as a valid exercise of constituent power
The Court struck down only the specific offending provisions, leaving the rest of the 42nd Amendment intact
The Court referred the matter back to Parliament without a ruling
advanced.e: The Supreme Court in Minerva Mills did not invalidate the whole 42nd Amendment; it invalidated only the specific clauses that conferred unlimited amending power and unlimited DPSP primacy over Fundamental Rights, as being destructive of the basic structure.

advanced.q: How did the original Article 31C, inserted by the 25th Amendment Act (1971), differ from the version introduced by the 42nd Amendment Act (1976), as relevant to the basic structure jurisprudence?
o: The 1971 version protected laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and (c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19, while the 1976 version extended this immunity to all Directive Principles
The 1971 version extended immunity to all Directive Principles, while the 1976 version restricted it to Article 39(b) and (c) alone
Both versions were identical in scope
The 1971 version was struck down by Kesavananda Bharati, while the 1976 version was upheld by Minerva Mills
advanced.e: The original Article 31C (25th Amendment, 1971) shielded only laws implementing Article 39(b) and (c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19, and this limited version was substantially upheld in Kesavananda Bharati; the 42nd Amendment widened this immunity to cover laws implementing all Directive Principles, and this wider version was struck down in Minerva Mills.

advanced.q: The doctrine of prospective overruling, as applied in the Golaknath case, had what practical effect?
o: It invalidated all past constitutional amendments retrospectively
It held the ruling would apply only to future amendments, leaving amendments already made (such as the 1st, 4th and 17th Amendments) undisturbed
It required Parliament to re-enact all prior amendments
It automatically extended to strike down the 24th Amendment before it was even enacted
advanced.e: By applying prospective overruling, the Court in Golaknath ensured that its ruling barring amendment of Fundamental Rights would operate only prospectively, thereby not disturbing amendments already validly made in the past.

advanced.q: Kesavananda Bharati, the petitioner in the 1973 case, had approached the Supreme Court primarily challenging which state legislation?
o: Kerala Agrarian Relations Act, 1961 alone, unrelated to land reforms
advanced.e: Kesavananda Bharati, head of the Edneer Mutt in Kerala, challenged the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act as violating his fundamental rights to manage religious property, which led the Court to examine the broader question of the extent of Parliament's amending power.

advanced.q: Which of the following features has NOT typically been cited by the Supreme Court as forming part of the basic structure?
o: Reservation percentage prescribed for a particular state
advanced.e: Features such as independence of judiciary, secularism, and federal character have been held to be part of the basic structure across various cases, whereas a state-specific reservation percentage is a policy matter, not a basic feature of the Constitution.

advanced.q: What is the key difference between the holdings of the Waman Rao case (1981) and the I.R. Coelho case (2007) regarding the Ninth Schedule?
o: Waman Rao dealt with unamendability of Fundamental Rights generally, while Coelho dealt exclusively with federal disputes

Waman Rao fixed 24 April 1973 as the cut-off date for applying the basic structure doctrine to amendments/Ninth Schedule insertions, while Coelho applied and reaffirmed this principle specifically to test post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws against the basic structure
Waman Rao declared the Ninth Schedule itself unconstitutional, which Coelho later reversed
There is no material difference; both cases were decided identically on identical facts
advanced.e: Waman Rao established that the basic structure doctrine applies prospectively from 24 April 1973, while Coelho built upon this by holding that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after that date must be tested for consistency with the basic structure and Fundamental Rights.

advanced.q: Chief Justice Y.V. Chandrachud's opinion in Minerva Mills famously described the Indian Constitution as founded on the bedrock of which principle?
o: Balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy
Unlimited judicial supremacy over the legislature
Strict separation between the Centre and the States
advanced.e: Chief Justice Chandrachud held that the Indian Constitution is founded on the bedrock of the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles, and that giving absolute primacy to one over the other would disturb the harmony essential to the basic structure.

advanced.q: Which of the following correctly reflects the evolving and non-exhaustive nature of the Basic Structure Doctrine?
o: The Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati provided a final, closed list of basic features that cannot be added to

Basic structure elements have been identified and expanded across multiple cases such as Indira Gandhi (free and fair elections, judicial review), Minerva Mills (harmony between FR and DPSP), and others, without an exhaustive definition
Only Fundamental Rights collectively constitute the basic structure, and no other constitutional feature qualifies
The doctrine was abandoned after Minerva Mills and has not been applied since 1980
advanced.e: The Basic Structure Doctrine has never been exhaustively defined; courts have progressively identified features such as free and fair elections and judicial review (Indira Gandhi case) and harmony between FR and DPSP (Minerva Mills) as part of the basic structure, and the doctrine continues to be invoked and refined, including in later cases like I.R. Coelho (2007).

title: Parliamentary System
desc: Executive-legislature relations, Cabinet government, key Articles

basic.q: Which Articles of the Constitution provide for a parliamentary system of government at the Union level?
basic.e: Article 74 provides for a Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President, and Article 75 deals with appointment, tenure and responsibility of ministers, together establishing the parliamentary system at the Union level.

basic.q: Which Articles provide for the parliamentary system of government at the State level?
basic.e: Article 163 provides for a Council of Ministers to aid and advise the Governor, and Article 164 deals with appointment and responsibility of state ministers, mirroring Articles 74 and 75 at the state level.

basic.q: In India's parliamentary system, who is the 'nominal executive'?
basic.e: The President is the constitutional/nominal head of state, while real executive power vests in the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister.

basic.q: Who constitutes the 'real executive' in India's parliamentary system?
o: The Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister
basic.e: The Council of Ministers, headed by the Prime Minister, exercises actual executive power and decision-making authority, even though the President is the formal head of state.

basic.q: The parliamentary system of government is also commonly known as the:
basic.e: The parliamentary system, based on the British pattern, is popularly called the Westminster model, also referred to as cabinet government or responsible government.

basic.q: The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to which body under Article 75(3)?
o: The Lok Sabha (House of the People)
basic.e: Article 75(3) states that the Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, meaning it stays in office only as long as it enjoys the confidence of that House.

basic.q: Under Article 75(5), a minister who is not a member of either House of Parliament ceases to be a minister after:
basic.e: Article 75(5) provides that a minister who is not a member of either House for a continuous period of six months ceases to be a minister at the expiration of that period.
